lessons.title: How To Get Your First Design Client
objectives: Name the people already in your network who could become a first client
Make a specific offer instead of announcing that you are available
Handle the no-track-record problem without working for free indefinitely
lessons.notes:
The hard part of client number one is not skill, it is that nobody can see evidence you can do the work. The way through is a specific offer to a specific person, not a broadcast. "I am available for design work" gets nothing. "I noticed your menu photos are hard to read on a phone — I can redo the menu as a clean PDF for KSh 3,000, and you can see a draft before you pay anything" gets replies.

Your first clients are almost always people who already know you: a relative's business, a church or mosque noticeboard, a former employer, a friend's side hustle, a shop you buy from. That is not a lesser route. It is how nearly every freelance career actually begins.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — free work, and where the line is. Doing one small piece free or cheap to get a testimonial and a portfolio piece is a reasonable investment, once or twice, with a clear end. Doing ongoing free work because someone keeps promising exposure is not. Set the boundary out loud before you start: "I will do this first one at KSh 2,000 so you can see how I work — after that my rate is X." Saying it in advance is what stops it becoming permanent.

Ask for two things when you finish: a written line you can quote, and permission to show the work. Both are worth more than the fee on your first job.
lessons.practice: Write down ten people or businesses you already have some connection to. For three of them, write a specific one-sentence offer naming a problem you have actually noticed and what you would charge. Send one of them today. The exercise only counts if you send it.

quiz.question: Why does a specific offer beat announcing that you are available?
options: It is shorter to write
It names a problem the person already recognises and tells them exactly what happens next, which is what earns a reply
It lets you charge more
Announcements are blocked by most platforms

quiz.question: What makes free work reasonable rather than a trap?
options: Doing it only for large companies
Keeping it under ten hours
A clear, stated end — one small piece for a testimonial and a portfolio right, with your rate named in advance
Never putting it in writing

lessons.title: 4 Ways To Get Your First 10 Customers
objectives: Compare four routes to early customers and pick the two that suit you
Judge a channel by whether your buyers are actually there
Keep a simple record of what you tried and what it produced
lessons.notes:
Getting to ten customers is a different problem from getting one. One comes from your network; ten needs something repeatable. This class lays out four routes — roughly: people you know, communities where your buyers already gather, direct outreach to strangers, and being findable when someone searches.

The filter that matters is not which route is best in general, but where YOUR buyers are. If you design for salons, the salon owners' WhatsApp groups and Instagram are the channel; LinkedIn is not. If you write for software companies, the reverse.

Pick two and work them properly for a month. Trying all four badly is the most common way to conclude that nothing works.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — the record that makes this learnable. Keep one sheet: date, who you contacted, which route, and what happened. After thirty entries you will be able to see which route actually produced replies rather than guessing. Almost no beginner does this, and it is the difference between six months of effort teaching you something and six months teaching you nothing.

On local channels specifically: Facebook groups for Kenyan small businesses, WhatsApp groups in your trade, and Instagram DMs are where a great deal of real work is arranged here. Do not dismiss them because international advice talks about LinkedIn and cold email.
lessons.practice: Choose two of the four routes. For each, write down exactly where your buyers gather — name the group, the hashtag, the platform. Then set up the tracking sheet with four columns (date, contact, route, outcome) and put your first five attempts in it this week.

quiz.question: How should you choose between the four routes?
options: Pick the one that works best for most freelancers
By where your particular buyers already gather
Start with the cheapest
Use all four at once

quiz.question: What is the point of the tracking sheet?
options: Clients expect to see it
It is required for tax purposes
After enough entries it shows which route actually produces replies, instead of leaving you to guess
It replaces a portfolio

lessons.title: How To Attract New Customers & Grow Your Freelance Business
objectives: Explain the difference between chasing work and building a system that attracts it
Identify one asset you can build that keeps working after you stop
Set a weekly rhythm you can sustain alongside paid work
lessons.notes:
This is a long class — watch it in two sittings if data is a concern. The central idea is the shift from hunting each job individually to building something that brings people to you: a body of public work, a reputation in one specific niche, a channel you post to consistently.

The catch nobody mentions: you build that while you are busy with paid work, which is exactly when you least want to. The freelancers who stay busy are the ones who keep a small weekly habit going during good months. The ones who lurch between famine and feast are the ones who only market when work runs out — by which point it is already too late, because attracting work has a lag of weeks.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — what a realistic weekly rhythm looks like here. Two hours, once a week, protected. One useful public post about the work you do, two direct approaches to people who fit your niche, and one follow-up with a past client. That is it. It is small enough to keep doing in a busy month, which is the only quality that matters.

Niche down further than feels comfortable. "Designer" competes with everyone; "menus and signage for Nairobi restaurants" competes with almost nobody and is far easier to be recommended for, because people can remember what you do.
lessons.practice: Write your niche as a single sentence in the form "I do [specific thing] for [specific kind of business]". Then block two hours in your calendar on a fixed day this week and do the four actions: one public post, two approaches, one follow-up. Put the same block in for the next three weeks now.

quiz.question: Why do freelancers who only market when work runs out struggle?
options: Clients can tell they are desperate
Attracting work has a lag of weeks, so starting when you are already empty means the gap is unavoidable
Marketing is more expensive in quiet months
Platforms reduce visibility for inactive accounts

quiz.question: Why narrow the niche further than feels comfortable?
options: Narrow niches allow higher hourly rates by law
It reduces the amount of work you have to do
People can remember what you do, which is what makes you recommendable
Broad freelancers are banned from most platforms

lessons.title: Win More Freelancing Clients with the Best Proposal Format
objectives: Structure a proposal that restates the client's problem before naming a price
Present pricing as options rather than a single figure
Remove the parts of a proposal that cause delay and doubt
lessons.notes:
A proposal is not a price list. Mike Janda's structure works because it spends most of its length proving you understood the problem, so that by the time the client reaches the number they are already nodding.

The move worth copying above all others is offering three options rather than one price. A single figure invites a yes-or-no; three options change the question to which one, and they let a client who cannot afford your full scope buy something smaller instead of disappearing.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — proposals for Kenyan and international clients. Two things to settle in writing before any work starts, because they cause more disputes than scope ever does. First, CURRENCY AND METHOD: are you being paid in KSh or USD, and through what — M-Pesa, bank transfer, Wise, Payoneer? Wise and Payoneer both work from Kenya and are how most freelancers here receive foreign payment; PayPal's ability to withdraw to Kenyan accounts has been restricted and unreliable, so do not assume it. Name the method in the proposal.

Second, A DEPOSIT. Half up front for a new client is normal and protects you from the most common loss in freelancing, which is not being paid at all. A client who refuses any deposit on a first job is telling you something useful.

Keep the document short. A two-page proposal sent today beats a ten-page one sent next week.
lessons.practice: Take a real or imagined job and write a proposal with four parts: what you understood the problem to be, what you propose to do, three priced options, and what happens next. Name the payment method and the deposit. Then cut it until it fits on two pages.

quiz.question: Why offer three priced options instead of one figure?
options: It makes the proposal look longer
It changes the question from yes-or-no to which one, and lets a client who cannot afford full scope buy something smaller
Clients are required to choose the middle option
It avoids having to discuss the problem

quiz.question: What should a proposal settle in writing besides scope and price?
options: Your availability for the next year
The client's marketing strategy
The currency, the payment method, and the deposit
The names of your other clients

lessons.title: How to Handle Scope Creep in Client Projects
objectives: Recognise scope creep in its early, polite form
Say yes to extra work in a way that attaches a price to it
Use the original agreement as the reference point rather than your memory
lessons.notes:
Scope creep almost never arrives as a demand. It arrives as "could you just" — small, reasonable-sounding, and cumulative. Three of those can add a week to a project you priced for three days.

The sentence that solves most of it is not a refusal. It is: "Yes, I can do that — it is outside what we agreed, so it would be an extra KSh X and push delivery to Friday. Shall I go ahead?" That answer is cooperative, it keeps the relationship intact, and it makes the cost visible at the moment the request is made rather than in a resentful conversation later.

This only works if there is a written agreement to refer to. Without one it becomes your word against theirs, and you will usually give way.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — revisions are where this bites hardest for beginners. State a number in the proposal: "includes two rounds of revisions; further rounds at KSh X each." Unlimited revisions is the single most common way a well-priced job becomes unpaid work, and clients are not being unreasonable in asking — they simply have no reason to stop if stopping was never defined.

When a client is a relative or a friend of the family, this matters more, not less. Write it down anyway, kindly and early. It is far easier than the conversation you will otherwise have at Christmas.
lessons.practice: Write your own version of the yes-and-price sentence, in your own words, and keep it somewhere you can copy it from. Then take any past or imagined job and write the two lines you would put in the agreement covering revisions and what counts as extra.

quiz.question: What is the most effective response to a scope-creep request?
options: Refuse it and cite the contract
Do it quietly to keep the client happy
Agree, and immediately name the extra cost and the new delivery date, asking whether to proceed
Delay answering until the project ends

quiz.question: Why does specifying a number of revision rounds matter so much?
options: Clients respect freelancers who limit revisions
Without a defined stopping point there is no reason for revisions to stop, which is how a well-priced job becomes unpaid work
More than two rounds is bad practice
It is a legal requirement in most contracts

lessons.title: You Need a Contract: Legal Basics for Freelancers
objectives: List the clauses a simple freelance agreement must contain
Explain why a written agreement protects the client too
Put an agreement in place without a lawyer or a large budget
lessons.notes:
A freelance agreement does not need to be long or expensive. It needs to answer six questions in writing: what you will deliver, by when, for how much, paid how and when, how many revisions are included, and who owns the work at the end.

That last one surprises people. Unless you say otherwise, ownership of what you produce is not automatically transferred simply because someone paid you, and disputes about reuse are common. Say plainly that ownership passes to the client on final payment — which also gives them a reason to make that payment.

A written agreement is not an act of distrust, and framing it that way to a nervous client helps: it protects them as much as you, because it is the only record of what they were promised.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — doing this practically in Kenya. An email exchange where you set out the six points and the client replies agreeing IS a written agreement, and is enormously better than nothing. You do not need a signed PDF or a lawyer to start. For anything substantial, a short signed document is better, and both parties keeping a copy matters.

If you are storing clients' customer data — names, phone numbers, photographs — the Data Protection Act applies to you as well as to them. Do not collect what you do not need, and be able to say where it is kept.

For international clients, note that chasing a small debt across borders is effectively impossible. That is the real reason for a deposit, not distrust.
lessons.practice: Write your own one-page agreement template answering the six questions, in plain language. Keep it as a document you can adapt in five minutes. Then write the short, friendly message you would send alongside it to a client who has never signed anything with a freelancer before.

quiz.question: Why state explicitly who owns the work at the end?
options: Ownership is otherwise split equally by law
Ownership does not transfer automatically just because someone paid, and reuse disputes are common
Clients cannot publish work without a clause
It is required before invoicing

quiz.question: Why is a deposit particularly important with an international client?
options: Foreign clients are less trustworthy
It is required by payment processors
Chasing a small debt across borders is effectively impossible, so the deposit is your only real protection
It reduces the currency conversion fee
